P0C8B.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor I Circuit High
P0C8B.description: P0C8B covers a sensor I signal stuck above its valid voltage, which the controller interprets as extreme cold. An interrupted circuit lets the pull-up lift the line, so the root cause is usually an open connection or a failed thermistor rather than the weather. On the 2016 Cadillac ELR (16OBDG01) GM fails it below −40 °C, an ADC count above 3992, for 1.4 s within 2 s, two trips. Mitsubishi's 2018 Outlander PHEV declares channel [08] open beyond 3.97 V, colder than −62 °C, held 2 s. For the Volt, bulletin 18-NA-342 lists it as sensor 9 circuit high voltage among codes that can come with a Battery Too Cold message above −25 °C and recommends new module software. The short-circuit counterpart is P0C8A.

causes.label: Open wire or loose connector in the sensor I circuit
Thermistor I open
Battery module software causing false cold readings (GM Volt, 18-NA-342)

symptoms: Battery-too-cold message although outside temperature is mild
Electric drive limited or unavailable
Battery heater running unnecessarily

P0C8C.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor I Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0C8C.description: P0C8C reports that sensor I changes faster and more often than any real battery temperature could. GM is the only maker that publishes the test: in 19OBDG02, the 2019 hybrid powertrain control module 2 table, each 10-sample window at 100 ms per sample is scored by the summed absolute change of the reading, a score above 10 counts as a failed window, and 4 failed windows out of 5 set the code, Type B, two trips, with system voltage above 10.2 V and no communication fault to the battery interface module. The 2018 table 18OBDG02 contains the same rule. Unlike P0C8A and P0C8B the value never leaves its valid range. Look for a fretting terminal or a wire broken inside its insulation; several erratic sensors at once point to the sensing board.

causes.label: Fretting or loose terminal on the sensor I connector
Sensor I wire broken inside its insulation
Sensing board with unstable supply or ground

symptoms: Warning lamp appearing now and then
Sensor I value jumping in live data
Short phases of reduced power

P0C8D.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor J Circuit
P0C8D.description: P0C8D covers electrical trouble in the circuit of battery temperature sensor J that the controller cannot pin down to a low, high or jumping signal. There is no public manufacturer documentation for P0C8D. GM's 2011 hybrid table counts J as temperature sensor 10 in a list of sixteen, yet like its later tables it only defines the narrower J codes P0C8E to P0C91; Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV assigns J to module sensor [09] and likewise uses only rationality, short and open codes. Under CARB rule (e)(15.3.1) every such input must be watched all the time for plausible values and an unbroken circuit. Without a valid J reading the battery management protects that cell group by cutting charge and discharge power.

causes.label: Corroded or loose plug between sensor J and the monitoring board
Thermistor J electrically defective
Faulty input channel on the cell monitoring board

symptoms: Hybrid system warning, on many models also the check-engine lamp
Less electric power and slower charging

P0C8E.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor J Circuit Range/Performance
P0C8E.description: P0C8E sets when sensor J delivers an electrically valid temperature that disagrees with the other modules. For the 2012 Volt, table 12OBDG01A runs the check only after propulsion, off-board charging and battery conditioning have all been inactive for more than 21,600 s, so the pack should be evenly soaked; a gap above 25.3 °C to the mean of the remaining sensors in 50 of 67 samples fails it, Type B. The 2019 GM table 19OBDG02 keeps the logic with a 25.00 °C limit. Mitsubishi, on the 2018 Outlander PHEV, calls it rationality of sensor [09] and accepts a much smaller gap of 13 °C once the car has stood for 3,600 s. A loosened sensor or a real hot spot is more likely than a wiring fault; P0C8F and P0C90 cover shorts and opens.

causes.label: Thermistor J drifted but still within its electrical range
Sensor J no longer pressed against its cell group
Actual temperature difference from a weak cell or blocked cooling path

symptoms: Warning lamp appearing after the car has been parked for many hours
Battery power reduced while the pack is cold or warm

P0C8F.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor J Circuit Low
P0C8F.description: P0C8F means the voltage on sensor J has dropped below its valid window. The NTC thermistor is powered via a pull-up resistor, so a grounded signal line reads as an absurdly hot cell group; low refers to the signal. GM's HPC2 table of 2019 (19OBDG02) converts the voltage and fails the test if the result is over 160 °C for 8 samples out of 10, sampled every 100 ms and rated Type B. The older 2012 Volt table judges all sensors together and fails them above 87.5 °C (raw count under 680) for 1.4 s of a 2 s window. On the 2018 Outlander PHEV, Mitsubishi logs a short of sensor [09] once the signal remains below 0.12 V, hotter than 125 °C, for 2 s. A genuinely overheating pack would instead set P0A7E. Expect reduced power and battery cooling running hard.

causes.label: Sensor J signal wire chafed and shorted to ground
Thermistor J shorted internally, for example after moisture
Monitoring board input pulling the line low

symptoms: Warning lamp with clearly reduced electric power
Battery fan or chiller running constantly
Engine starts more often on plug-in hybrids

P0C90.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor J Circuit High
P0C90.description: P0C90 reports the opposite case: sensor J reads above its voltage window, which with a pull-up circuit points to an open thermistor, a broken lead or a disconnected plug, and the controller sees an impossibly cold module. In GM's 2016 and 2019 tables (16OBDG02, 19OBDG02) a converted value colder than −69 °C in 8 out of 10 readings, one every 100 ms, fails the test; it is Type B, so the lamp waits for the second bad trip, and it runs only above 10.2 V with communication intact. For sensor [09] of the 2018 Outlander PHEV, Mitsubishi records an open when more than 3.97 V, below −62 °C, persists for 2 s. Because the battery seems frozen, the system may limit power, keep the engine running or ask for warming on a plug-in. P0C8F is the short-circuit counterpart.

causes.label: Open lead or unplugged connector at sensor J
Thermistor J open internally
Terminal pushed back in the monitoring board plug

symptoms: Battery-too-cold message although the weather is mild
Little or no electric drive power
Battery heater switching on without need

P0C91.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor J Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0C91.description: P0C91 watches for a sensor J reading that changes too fast and too often for a heavy battery. GM's tables 16OBDG02 and 19OBDG02 add up how far the value moves between samples over a 10-sample window taken every 100 ms; a sum above 10 fails the window, and 4 failing windows out of 5, about half a second, store the code, Type B over two trips. The check needs more than 10.2 V and working communication. The reading may stay within its valid range, which distinguishes P0C91 from P0C8F and P0C90. Mitsubishi's PHEV has nothing comparable for this channel. Likely culprits are a worn contact or a conductor broken under its insulation; if neighbouring sensors jump at the same moment, suspect the monitoring board.

causes.label: Fretting or loose terminal in the sensor J plug
Conductor broken inside the insulation, opening under vibration
Unstable reference or ground on the monitoring board

symptoms: Warning lamp that comes and goes between drives
Sensor J value jumping in live data

P0C92.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor K Circuit
P0C92.description: P0C92 is stored when the input from battery temperature sensor K has an electrical fault that the controller leaves unclassified. Public manufacturer documentation for exactly this code does not exist. In GM's 2011 rationality list K appears as sensor 11 of sixteen, and GM's later hybrid tables from 2012 up to 19OBDG02 only define the specific K codes P0C93 to P0C96. Mitsubishi maps K to module sensor [10] on its plug-in Outlander and there, too, distinguishes only rationality, short and open. The legal basis is CARB paragraph (e)(15.3.1), which calls for permanent checks of plausible values and wiring continuity. Diagnosis covers the thermistor, its leads and the plug at the monitoring board, all inside the traction battery, after it has been made safe.

causes.label: Poor contact at the sensor K plug
Thermistor K failed
Defective input channel on the cell monitoring board

symptoms: Hybrid or EV warning message
Reduced electric power until the fault is repaired

P0C93.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor K Circuit Range/Performance
P0C93.description: P0C93 compares sensor K with its neighbours: the reading is electrically fine but too far from the pack average. GM's 2016 hybrid table 16OBDG02 sets it when the absolute difference exceeds 25.00 °C for 50 samples out of 67 taken every 25 ms, roughly 1.7 s, rated Type B; the check is suspended whenever a low, high or erratic code for the battery sensors is active. GM's 2011 table lists K as sensor 11. Mitsubishi handles it on the 2018 Outlander PHEV as a rationality fault of sensor [10]: it needs 3,600 s of soak, a pack temperature from −30 to 60 °C and a 13 °C deviation lasting 0.32 s, tested once per drive. A thermistor that drifted or lost contact with its cells is the typical finding.

causes.label: Thermistor K reading off while still electrically valid
Sensor K lifted off its cell group
Real temperature spread from uneven coolant flow or a weak cell

symptoms: Warning lamp, often first noticed after a cold start
Charging and discharging power limited

P0C94.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor K Circuit Low
P0C94.description: With P0C94 the controller sees the sensor K signal pulled below its lower limit, a pattern produced by a chafed wire touching ground or an internally shorted thermistor, which the conversion turns into an extreme temperature. GM's 2016 table 16OBDG02 counts a failure whenever the converted value is hotter than 160 °C and needs 8 such readings out of 10, one every 100 ms, Type B; in the 2012 Volt table the same sensor group passes only at or below 87.5 °C. The 2018 Outlander PHEV from Mitsubishi files a short of sensor [10] when the voltage stays below 0.12 V for 2 s. Unlike with the over-temperature code P0A7E, the pack itself is usually not hot. The battery controller nonetheless limits power and may keep the cooling busy; the open-circuit partner is P0C95.

causes.label: Sensor K signal line shorted to ground
Thermistor K shorted internally
Moisture or coolant reaching the sensor K connection

symptoms: Warning lamp and reduced electric power
Battery cooling running although the pack is not hot

P0C95.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor K Circuit High
P0C95.description: P0C95 is set when sensor K delivers a voltage above its valid range. In the usual NTC layout a broken circuit allows the bias resistor to drive the input high, so the controller sees an impossibly cold module. In 19OBDG02 (GM, 2019) a reading colder than −69 °C in 8 out of 10 checks counts as failed, Type B; the 2012 Volt table accepts readings only down to −40 °C, equal to an ADC count of 4,000. Mitsubishi names it an open of sensor [10] on the 2018 Outlander PHEV, above 3.97 V for 2 s. Look for a pushed-out terminal, a broken wire or an unplugged connector before replacing parts. Drivers may see reduced electric power or a warning that the battery is too cold. P0C94 is the matching short-circuit code.

causes.label: Open circuit or disconnected plug at sensor K
Thermistor K open internally
Sensor lead damaged during earlier work on the pack

symptoms: Battery-too-cold or plug-in-to-warm message in mild weather
Electric power reduced or unavailable

P0C96.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor K Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0C96.description: P0C96 flags an unsteady sensor K signal, the kind of noise a loose contact produces while the value still sits inside its valid band. GM describes the monitor in 16OBDG02 and 18OBDG02: each 100 ms sample adds to a running total of absolute changes across 10 samples, a total above 10 marks the window as failed, and 4 failed windows in 5 store the code, Type B, so two bad trips are needed. Supply over 10.2 V and intact communication with the battery interface module are prerequisites. Mitsubishi defines no erratic code for its sensor [10]. Moving the harness by hand while a scan tool shows the value often reveals the cause. P0C94 and P0C95 cover faults where the signal stays out of range.

causes.label: Loose contact in the sensor K connector
Partly chafed sensor lead touching intermittently
Monitoring board with unstable supply or ground

symptoms: Intermittent warning lamp
Short spells of reduced power

P0C97.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor L Circuit
P0C97.description: P0C97 is the catch-all for battery temperature sensor L, used when the input misbehaves electrically but fits none of the low, high or erratic categories. No manufacturer publishes this exact code. GM's 2011 hybrid table counts L as temperature sensor 12 of sixteen, and its 2012 and later tables cover L only with P0C98 to P0C9B. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV DTC list goes from sensor [10] (P0C93 to P0C95) straight to sensor [12] (P0CA9 onward), so it uses no L codes at all. CARB paragraph (e)(15.3.1) demands constant supervision of plausibility and circuit integrity for inputs like this. A pack controller that loses sensor L assumes a worst-case temperature for that section and reduces available power until the fault is repaired.

causes.label: Connector fault between sensor L and the monitoring board
Thermistor L defective
Faulty measuring channel on the monitoring board

symptoms: Hybrid or EV warning, possibly with check-engine lamp
Limited battery power

P0C98.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor L Circuit Range/Performance
P0C98.description: P0C98 is the plausibility code for sensor L: its reading is electrically valid but strays too far from the other sensors. GM's table for the 2012 Volt (12OBDG01A) runs the comparison only after more than 21,600 s with propulsion, off-board charging and thermal conditioning all off; a deviation over 25.3 °C, seen in 50 of 67 samples, counts as a Type B failure. In 19OBDG02 from 2019 the limit becomes 25.00 °C with sampling every 25 ms and the same count, and the test pauses while circuit codes for the battery sensors or a lost link to the battery controller are present. Mitsubishi does not use this code. Sensor drift or a detached sensor are the common reasons; P0C99 and P0C9A cover electrical failures.

causes.label: Thermistor L drifted within its electrical range
Sensor L no longer in thermal contact with its cells
Genuine local temperature difference in that pack section

symptoms: Warning lamp after a long standstill
Reduced battery power

P0C99.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor L Circuit Low
P0C99.description: P0C99 reports a sensor L voltage below the valid range. Because the thermistor works against a bias resistor on its monitoring board, any ground fault or an internally shorted sensor drags the voltage down, which reads as a very hot module. GM's 2019 HPC2 table 19OBDG02 flags it once the converted value exceeds 160 °C in 8 out of 10 readings at 100 ms intervals; it is a Type B code and needs supply above 10.2 V. The 2012 Volt table groups L with the other sensors and passes them only at or below 87.5 °C, which equals a raw count of 680 or more, and needs 1.4 s out of 2 s to fail. Mitsubishi does not use L codes. If the pack is really overheating, P0A7E appears instead. Expect a warning lamp and reduced battery power.

causes.label: Sensor L signal shorted to ground
Thermistor L shorted internally
Monitoring board channel pulling the input low

symptoms: Warning lamp and reduced battery power
Battery cooling running for no apparent reason

P0C9A.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor L Circuit High
P0C9A.description: P0C9A is the high-voltage fault of sensor L: an open thermistor, a broken lead or a disconnected plug lets the bias resistor raise the input, and the reading looks like deep frost. GM's 2016 table 16OBDG02 sets it when 8 readings out of 10, taken every 100 ms, are colder than −69 °C; it is Type B and requires more than 10.2 V supply plus working communication. The 2012 Volt table treats readings below −40 °C, a raw count above 4,000, as failed. Mitsubishi assigns no code to sensor L. The controller then plans for a frozen battery, so electric power can be reduced and a plug-in may run its battery heater or engine. Check the plug at the monitoring board first; P0C99 is the short-circuit partner.

causes.label: Open circuit or unplugged connector at sensor L
Thermistor L open internally
Corroded terminal with very high contact resistance

symptoms: Battery-too-cold indication in mild conditions
Electric power reduced, engine running more on plug-ins

P0C9B.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor L Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0C9B.description: P0C9B covers a sensor L signal that jitters. GM's tables 18OBDG02 and 19OBDG02 integrate the absolute sample-to-sample changes over ten readings spaced 100 ms apart; when the integral exceeds 10, that window fails, and 4 failures within 5 windows store the code, classed Type B. Supply must exceed 10.2 V and communication with the battery interface module must be present. Because the value may never leave its valid band, P0C99 and P0C9A can stay silent. Mitsubishi does not use this code. A fretting pin, a cracked conductor or a loose board ground are typical, and the fault may vanish between drives, so freeze-frame data and a wiggle test help to find it.

causes.label: Fretting pin in the sensor L connector
Cracked conductor in the sensor L lead
Loose ground on the cell monitoring board

symptoms: Warning lamp that may switch off again by itself
Erratic sensor L value in live data

P0C9C.title: 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor B Circuit
P0C9C.description: P0C9C flags an electrical problem, not further classified, with current sensor B of the 14 volt power module, the DC/DC converter that supplies the 12 V network from the high-voltage battery; GM calls it the accessory power module (APM). In GM's 2013 eAssist table sensor B is the APM output current sensor, while sensor A (P0A86 to P0A8A) measures the input side. No manufacturer documents P0C9C publicly; GM uses only the low and high codes P0C9E and P0C9F plus the A/B correlation code P0CC5. CARB rule (e)(15.3.1) calls for continuous range and continuity monitoring of such inputs. With no trustworthy output current the converter may be derated, and the 12 V battery can slowly discharge. The sensor normally sits inside the module.

causes.label: Current sensor B inside the power module failed
Poor contact at the power module signal connector
Control software of the power module or hybrid controller

symptoms: Warning lamp, sometimes a charging-system message
12 V battery running low over time

P0C9D.title: 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P0C9D.description: P0C9D means the output current reported by sensor B of the 14 V power module is electrically valid but implausible for the operating state. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM's 2013 eAssist table checks this kind of plausibility through the correlation code P0CC5 instead: the output power derived from sensor B is compared with the input power from sensor A multiplied by an efficiency factor between 0.90 and 0.99, and a gap above 0.4 kW for 3.75 s within 5 s sets it, Type B. That test is blocked while P0C9E or P0C9F is active. A sensor with offset or gain drift is the usual reason, rarely a converter whose real output deviates. The driver may notice only a warning lamp or a 12 V battery that stays low.

causes.label: Offset or gain drift of current sensor B
Converter output really differing from the commanded power
High resistance at the 12 V output cable or ground

symptoms: Warning lamp without obvious driveability change
12 V battery charge state remaining low

P0C9E.title: 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor B Circuit Low
P0C9E.description: P0C9E is set when current sensor B of the 14 V power module reads too little. GM documents it for the eAssist accessory power module in its 2013 table 13OBDG05C: the APM output current measured by the sensor must stay below 2 A for 1.5 s, counted as 60 of 80 samples at 25 ms, with the vehicle in run/crank; the code is Type B, so the MIL comes on after the second failing trip. Since an operating converter feeds considerably more current to the 12 V side, such a reading points to an open signal path, a grounded signal line or a dead sensor. The input-side counterpart is P0A88, the high fault P0C9F. Without valid current data the system may restrict the converter, and the 12 V battery can run down.

causes.label: Output current sensor B failed inside the module
Sensor signal open or shorted to ground
Converter not delivering output although enabled

symptoms: Check-engine lamp after two drives
Low 12 V voltage, flickering lights or warning messages

P0C9F.title: 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor B Circuit High
P0C9F.description: P0C9F reports an output current from sensor B of the 14 V power module that exceeds what the converter can plausibly supply. GM's 2013 eAssist table 13OBDG05C sets it once the APM output current reading tops 123 A while calculated APM input power is between 0.25 and 1.8 kW, supply voltage is 9 to 32 V and the vehicle is in run/crank; 1.5 s out of a 2 s window fail it, Type B, two trips. Pairing a very high current with modest input power separates a sensor fault from a genuine heavy load. A signal shorted to voltage or an internal sensor defect is typical. P0C9E is the low counterpart, P0A89 the input sensor's high code, and P0CC5 compares both sensors.

causes.label: Internal defect of output current sensor B
Sensor signal shorted to a voltage source
Poor ground of the power module shifting the reading

symptoms: Check-engine lamp
Converter output reduced, 12 V battery discharging

P0CA0.title: 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor B Circuit Intermittent
P0CA0.description: P0CA0 covers short dropouts or spikes in the signal of current sensor B, the output-side sensor of the 14 V power module (DC/DC converter) in GM's numbering. Between the events the reading looks normal, which separates it from the hard low and high faults P0C9E and P0C9F. No manufacturer documents P0CA0 publicly; GM's eAssist table only lists fixed limits for this sensor, below 2 A and above 123 A, each judged over 1.5 s in 2 s, and the cross-check P0CC5. CARB paragraph (e)(15.3.1) still expects such inputs to be monitored without pause. Vibration, a loose module connector, corroded grounds or poor 12 V cable connections are the first things to inspect; freeze-frame data helps to catch the moment.

causes.label: Loose or fretting connector at the power module
Corroded ground or 12 V output connection
Current sensor B failing intermittently inside the module

symptoms: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Occasional dim lights or voltage messages

P0CA1.title: Drive Motor Control Module Requested MIL Illumination
P0CA1.description: P0CA1 is a request code, not a component fault: the drive motor control module has detected an emissions-relevant fault of its own and asks the engine control module to light the MIL, which stores P0CA1. Subaru documents this on the 2014 XV Crosstrek Hybrid in bulletin 07-82-14R: P0CA1 sits in the engine module and C1424 in the stability control module, both MIL requests comparable to P0700. They usually accompany the drive motor module codes P0CDD and P0A3F, which set when the 12 V auxiliary battery voltage drops; with those codes in history, reprogramming the drive motor module is the fix, and Subaru changed its logic in production from January 2014. If only P0CA1 and C1424 are present, diagnose per the service manual.

causes.label: Emissions-relevant fault stored in the drive motor control module
Module software reacting to a low 12 V battery (Subaru 07-82-14R)
Weak or discharged 12 V auxiliary battery

symptoms: Check-engine lamp, often with further warning lamps such as stability control
Hybrid drive behaving normally or with reduced electric assistance

P0CA2.title: DC/DC Converter Step Down Voltage Performance
P0CA2.description: P0CA2 means the step-down function of the DC/DC converter, which brings high-voltage battery power down to the 12 V network, is not working correctly. GM's 2013 eAssist table 13OBDG05C uses it for a shoot-through fault inside the 14 volt power module: if the module detects a failed silicon power switch, a single 25 ms detection at 9 to 32 V sets the code as Type A, so the MIL lights on the first trip. Documents GM supplied to NHTSA in recall query RQ13-003 on the 2013 Malibu mild hybrid show P0CA2 in dealer cases together with P0562 for low system voltage, power pack replacements, and engineering reviews of returned parts with no fault found. P0CA3 is the step-up counterpart. Without the converter the 12 V battery drains.

causes.label: Failed power semiconductor in the converter's step-down stage
Internal fault of the power module or power pack assembly
Spurious detection without a hardware fault, for example after supply dips

symptoms: Check-engine lamp on the first trip, often with a charging warning
Falling 12 V voltage, low-voltage codes such as P0562
Hybrid assistance or auto-stop unavailable

P0CA3.title: DC/DC Converter Step Up Voltage Performance
P0CA3.description: P0CA3 says the boost stage of a DC/DC converter fails to lift its output to the voltage the controller has requested. In full hybrids this stage, often called a boost or variable voltage converter, raises the traction battery voltage to a higher bus level that feeds the inverters. No manufacturer documents P0CA3 on a publicly reachable official server. A Ford patent, US20140252849A1, describes the typical check: a converter voltage is commanded, the gap to the measured value is watched over a calibratable period, and a lasting gap above a threshold produces a diagnostic signal. CARB section (e)(15.2.3) obliges manufacturers to monitor such hybrid components. P0CA2 is the step-down partner, P0A94 the broader converter performance code. Drivers usually notice reduced electric power and a hybrid warning.

causes.label: Failed power transistor or driver in the boost stage
Internal fault of the inverter/converter assembly, e.g. reactor or capacitor
Wrong reading from the voltage sensor before or after the boost stage
Stored as a consequence of another hybrid system fault

symptoms: Hybrid system warning with check-engine lamp
Noticeably reduced electric drive power or limp mode
Engine running more often than usual

P0CA4.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Charging Voltage High
P0CA4.description: P0CA4 is stored when the traction battery voltage climbs above its permitted limit while energy flows into the pack, for instance because a charger or the drive keeps pushing current although the cells are already full. Audi lists the code in TSB 2062631/5 from 2024 for the e-tron and Q8 e-tron family, there stored by the high-voltage charger module J1050 and described as an excessive battery load voltage. In that case it is one of several ghost entries produced by charger software, found without any customer complaint, and the bulletin says it can be ignored. CARB section (e)(15.2.3) requires monitoring of the energy storage system and of the onboard charger of plug-in vehicles. A real overvoltage normally appears together with cell codes such as P0DE7, and charging is then interrupted.

causes.label: Charger or battery control software storing a false entry (Audi 2062631/5)
Charging current not reduced in time as the pack approaches full charge
Faulty pack or cell voltage measurement in the battery management

symptoms: Charging stops early or does not start
Code found during a check without any noticeable symptom

P0CA5.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Discharging Voltage High
P0CA5.description: P0CA5 concerns a battery voltage judged too high while the pack is discharging, that is while it supplies the drive motor or other high-voltage consumers. Under load the terminal voltage normally sags, so an excessive value in this state points more to a measurement or plausibility fault than to genuine overcharge. No manufacturer documents P0CA5 publicly. CARB section (e)(15.2.3)(A) demands monitoring of the energy storage system, explicitly including the battery voltage sensors used as its inputs. The charging counterpart P0CA4 shows up in an Audi e-tron charger bulletin as a software ghost entry, so a software check is worthwhile here as well. Useful related checks are the pack voltage code P0AFB and the cell voltage code P0DE7. The battery controller will usually limit power until the cause is found.

causes.label: Faulty pack voltage sensing in the battery management
Battery or hybrid control software evaluating the voltage wrongly
Loose or corroded high-voltage or sense connection

symptoms: Hybrid or EV warning, often with check-engine lamp
Limited battery power output

P0CA6.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Charging Current High
P0CA6.description: P0CA6 flags a current into the traction battery that exceeds what the control system expects. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV (2018 and 2022) stores it in the PHEV-ECU when, in charging mode, the measured battery current stays above the calculated charger output request for 5 s; suspects are the BMU, the onboard charger/DC-DC converter and the PHEV-ECU, and the repair is confirmed with drive cycle pattern 7. Stellantis sees the code in the battery pack control module (BPCM): a 2023 STAR case for the Wrangler 4xe points to BPCM software, and bulletin 08-025-25 for the 2025 Dodge Charger EV brings charging-related changes against false P0CA6 entries, there combined with P167B and no Drive Ready. P0CA7 is the discharging counterpart.

causes.label: Battery control module software (Stellantis S2308000117, 08-025-25)
Onboard charger or DC-DC converter delivering more current than requested
Pack current sensor or battery management unit reading wrongly
Fault in the hybrid/PHEV control unit

symptoms: Check-engine lamp, often found after charging
Charging interrupted or not possible
Vehicle not entering ready mode on some EVs

P0CA7.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Discharging Current High
P0CA7.description: P0CA7 is set when more current flows out of the hybrid or EV battery than the controller allows. Audi documents it on 48 V mild hybrids (A6, A7, A8, later also Q7, Q8 and S/RS versions, 2018 to 2024): the battery management of the 48 V battery, J1120, stores P0CA700 as discharge current too high, often with U046900 in the engine module, and the cluster shows an electrical system warning. Audi's 2020 bulletin 2058831/1 fixes it with new software for the belt starter generator; revision 9 from 2023 adds a hardware test of that generator. Stellantis lists P0CA7-00 in bulletin 08-054-22 for the 2021 Wrangler 4xe among codes that light the MIL falsely and are cured by a battery pack control module flash. P0CA6 covers the charging direction.

causes.label: Starter/generator or battery module software (Audi 2058831, Stellantis 08-054-22)
Belt starter generator drawing excessive current
Battery current sensor or battery management misreading

symptoms: Electrical system or battery warning in the cluster
Start-stop or electric assistance temporarily unavailable
Check-engine lamp on plug-in hybrids

P0CA8.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor M Circuit
P0CA8.description: P0CA8 is the general circuit code for battery temperature sensor M, meant for electrical faults that the controller does not sort into low, high or erratic. No manufacturer publishes this exact code. In GM's 2011 Volt table the rationality list gives M the thirteenth of sixteen positions, yet GM only defines P0CA9 to P0CAC for it. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV assigns M to module sensor [12] and also uses only the rationality, short and open codes. CARB section (e)(15.3.1) requires continuous checks of range and continuity for inputs of this kind. Without a usable value the battery controller must assume a hot module section and restricts power. Repair means opening the made-safe traction battery and checking the sensor, its leads and the plug at the monitoring board.

causes.label: Poor contact at the plug of sensor M on the monitoring board
Thermistor M damaged
Faulty input channel of the cell monitoring board

symptoms: Hybrid or EV warning, possibly with check-engine lamp
Electric power reduced until repaired

P0CA9.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor M Circuit Range/Performance
P0CA9.description: P0CA9 reports that sensor M stays within its electrical limits yet disagrees with what the remaining pack sensors measure. GM's 2012 Volt table 12OBDG01A only runs the comparison once drive system, plug-in charging and battery conditioning have rested for over 21,600 s; a spread above 25.3 °C from the mean in 50 of 67 samples is a Type B failure. The 2018 HPC2 table 18OBDG02 uses 25.00 °C at 25 ms sampling and is suspended whenever circuit faults of the sensors or a communication loss with the battery interface module exist. Mitsubishi uses P0CA9 for module sensor [12] of the Outlander PHEV: after more than 3,600 s soak and at pack temperatures from −30 to 60 °C, a deviation of 13 °C or more from the mean of all 50 sensors for 0.32 s sets it. Drift or a loose sensor is typical.

causes.label: Thermistor M drifting while staying in its electrical range
Sensor M lost thermal contact with its module
Module section genuinely warmer or colder, e.g. cooling fault or weak cell

symptoms: Warning lamp appearing after a long parking period
Battery power limited

P0CAA.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor M Circuit Low
P0CAA.description: P0CAA means the voltage at sensor M has dropped below its valid band. Sensor M is an NTC element supplied via a bias resistor on the board, so a grounded lead or a shorted element drags the voltage down and reads as an extremely hot spot. GM's 2018 HPC2 table 18OBDG02 fails the test once the converted temperature exceeds 160 °C in 8 of 10 readings taken every 100 ms, Type B, with more than 10.2 V supply. The 2011 Volt table set it above 87.5 °C, a raw count below 680, held for 1.4 s within 2 s over two trips. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV calls it a short of sensor [12]: below 0.12 V, roughly above 125 °C, for 2 s; the remedy there is a new battery module or cell monitoring unit. A real overheating shows as P0A7E instead.

causes.label: Sensor M signal shorted to ground inside the pack
Thermistor M internally shorted
Measuring input of the cell monitoring unit defective

symptoms: Warning lamp with strongly reduced battery power
Battery cooling running without reason

P0CAB.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor M Circuit High
P0CAB.description: P0CAB is logged when the input of sensor M rises beyond its upper voltage limit. If the thermistor, one of its wires or the plug opens up, the pull-up resistor lifts the input, and the controller reads a temperature far below anything plausible. GM's HPC2 table 18OBDG02 sets it when 8 of 10 readings at 100 ms intervals are colder than −69 °C, as a Type B fault needing over 10.2 V and intact communication. In the 2011 Volt table the limit was −40 °C, a raw count above 4,000, held 1.4 s within 2 s, and a single trip was enough. Mitsubishi treats it as an open circuit of sensor [12] on the Outlander PHEV: above 3.97 V, below about −62 °C, for 2 s. A plug-in may then heat its battery needlessly or start the engine; P0CAA is the low partner.

causes.label: Open circuit or unplugged connector of sensor M
Thermistor M open internally
Corroded or spread terminal at the monitoring board

symptoms: Battery shown as very cold in mild weather
Reduced electric power, engine running more on plug-ins

P0CAC.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor M Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0CAC.description: P0CAC catches a sensor M signal that jumps around without necessarily leaving its permitted band. GM's HPC2 tables (16OBDG02 to 19OBDG02) add up the absolute changes between successive samples over a ten-sample window at 100 ms; whenever that total passes 10 the window is marked bad, and four bad windows in five lead to a Type B code after two trips. The test runs with more than 10.2 V supply and needs a working link to the battery interface module. Since the value may stay within limits, the hard codes P0CAA and P0CAB can remain silent. Mitsubishi has no jitter code for its pack sensors. Fretting contacts, a cracked conductor on the board or vibration-sensitive wiring are the usual reasons; wiggle tests with live data and freeze-frame records help to localise the fault.

causes.label: Fretting or loose contact in the sensor M circuit
Cracked conductor or solder joint on the monitoring board
Unstable ground of the monitoring board

symptoms: Warning lamp that may go out again on its own
Jumping sensor M value in live data

P0CAD.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor N Circuit
P0CAD.description: P0CAD stands for an electrical problem with battery temperature sensor N that the controller cannot assign to a specific failure type. Public manufacturer documentation for this exact code does not exist. GM's 2011 hybrid rationality list places N fourteenth among sixteen sensors, while its tables from 2012 onward cover N only with the specific codes P0CAE to P0CB1. On the plug-in Outlander, Mitsubishi equates N with module sensor [13] and likewise separates only rationality, short and open. CARB section (e)(15.3.1) is the basis for permanent monitoring of such input circuits. A pack controller without this reading has to plan conservatively for that section. Because the sensor lives inside the traction battery, checks are made only after the high-voltage system has been isolated.

causes.label: Connector or wire fault between sensor N and the monitoring board
Thermistor N defective
Faulty input channel of the cell monitoring board

symptoms: Hybrid or EV system message
Battery power reduced until repaired

P0CAE.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor N Circuit Range/Performance
P0CAE.description: P0CAE is the plausibility check for sensor N: the value is electrically acceptable, yet out of line with its neighbours. GM's 2012 Volt table 12OBDG01A demands a rest of more than 21,600 s without propulsion, external charging or thermal conditioning and then fails the test at a deviation above 25.3 °C in 50 of 67 samples, Type B. The 2019 table 19OBDG02 keeps the count but uses 25.00 °C, 25 ms sampling and a minimum supply of 10.2 V. Mitsubishi's 2022 Outlander PHEV applies the code to module sensor [13] and checks it once per drive cycle after a one-hour soak: 13 °C or more away from the 50-sensor mean for 0.32 s. Electrical faults of N are reported separately as P0CAF and P0CB0.

causes.label: Thermistor N reading off while electrically valid
Sensor N detached from its cell or module surface
Real temperature difference in that pack section

symptoms: Warning lamp after the car has stood for hours
Limited battery power

P0CAF.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor N Circuit Low
P0CAF.description: P0CAF sets when the signal of sensor N is pulled under its lower voltage limit. A ground fault in the lead or a shorted thermistor causes this, and because the NTC sensor works against a pull-up resistor the controller interprets it as an implausibly hot module. GM's 2017 HPC2 table 17OBDG02 records a failure once the computed temperature tops 160 °C in 8 of 10 readings, classed as Type B, provided the supply is above 10.2 V and code U179C is not active. The 2012 Volt table accepts N up to 87.5 °C, equal to a raw value from 680 upward. On the Outlander PHEV, Mitsubishi calls it a short of sensor [13], judged below 0.12 V for 2 s and fixed by replacing the battery module or cell monitoring unit. Genuine pack overheating is reported as P0A7E.

causes.label: Sensor N lead shorted to ground
Thermistor N internally shorted
Measuring input of the cell monitoring unit defective

symptoms: Warning lamp and markedly reduced battery power
Battery cooling running at full effort

P0CB0.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor N Circuit High
P0CB0.description: P0CB0 reports a sensor N input above its upper voltage limit, which a pack controller reads as an unrealistically cold module. The NTC sensor is biased by a pull-up resistor, so any interruption in the element, its leads or its plug makes the input rise. GM's 2018 HPC2 table 18OBDG02 lists P0CB0 by name as sensor N circuit high and fails it when 8 of 10 readings at 100 ms are below −69 °C, Type B, two trips; the 2016 table 16OBDG02 uses the same limit and blocks the test while U179C is set. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV DTC chart names it the open circuit of sensor [13], judged above 3.97 V, below about −62 °C, for 2 s. Assuming a frozen pack, the controller cuts electric power and plug-ins may switch on heating or the engine. Shorts are covered by P0CAF.

causes.label: Open lead or disconnected plug of sensor N
Thermistor N open internally
Corroded terminal at the monitoring board

symptoms: Battery reported as far too cold in mild conditions
Less electric range or power, engine starting more often

P0CB1.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor N Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0CB1.description: P0CB1 points to an unsteady sensor N signal rather than a lasting short or open. GM's 2019 table 19OBDG02 evaluates windows of ten samples, one every 100 ms, by integrating the absolute value of each change; above 10 the window counts as failed, and 4 failed windows within 5 set the code, Type B, two trips. It needs more than 10.2 V supply and an active data link to the battery interface control module. The 2016 table 16OBDG02 already ran this jitter test, there with U179C as a blocking code. Mitsubishi assigns no erratic code to sensor [13]. Because readings can stay inside the valid band, P0CAF and P0CB0 often remain absent. Loose pins, a damaged sensor lead or a cracked board track are likely, and the fault may come and go with temperature or vibration.

causes.label: Loose or fretting pin in the sensor N circuit
Chafed or partly broken sensor N lead
Cracked track on the monitoring board

symptoms: Intermittent warning lamp
Sensor N value jumping in live data

P0CB2.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor O Circuit
P0CB2.description: P0CB2 is the catch-all electrical code for battery temperature sensor O, reserved for circuit faults that are not classified as low, high or erratic. Publicly, no manufacturer documents this exact code. Counting the rationality list in GM's 2011 Volt table puts O in position 15 of 16, but GM only uses P0CB3 to P0CB6 for it. Mitsubishi maps O to module sensor [14] of the Outlander PHEV and likewise relies on the rationality, short and open codes alone. CARB section (e)(15.2.3)(A)(iv) counts battery temperature sensors among the inputs that have to be monitored, and (A)(v) asks for codes that point to the smallest replaceable unit. With O unusable, the controller has to guess the module temperature and normally cuts battery power. The thermistor sits inside the pack, so repair is a high-voltage job.

causes.label: Poor contact at the sensor O connector on the monitoring board
Damaged lead between thermistor O and the board
Faulty measuring channel in the cell monitoring unit

symptoms: Hybrid or EV system warning, possibly with check-engine lamp
Reduced electric power or charging rate

P0CB3.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor O Circuit Range/Performance
P0CB3.description: P0CB3 is a plausibility code: sensor O delivers an electrically valid reading, yet it strays too far from the rest of the pack. In GM's 2012 Volt table 12OBDG01A the check waits until propulsion, plug-in charging and battery thermal conditioning have all been off for more than 21,600 s; a gap above 25.3 °C to the average in 50 of 67 samples then counts as a Type B failure. The HPC2 tables 18OBDG02 and 19OBDG02 use 25.00 °C, sample every 25 ms and pause while sensor circuit faults or a communication loss with the battery electronics are present. Mitsubishi assigns P0CB3 to module sensor [14] of the Outlander PHEV and fails it at a deviation of 13 °C or more held for 0.32 s, after a soak above 3,600 s and with the pack between −30 and 60 °C.

causes.label: Thermistor O drifting while its voltage stays in range
Sensor O no longer seated firmly against its module
Module section really warmer or colder, e.g. weak cell or uneven cooling

symptoms: Warning lamp typically appearing after the car has stood for hours
Battery power limited

P0CB4.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor O Circuit Low
P0CB4.description: P0CB4 reports a signal voltage of sensor O below its lower limit. The sensor is an NTC thermistor biased by a resistor on the measuring board, so a short to ground or a shorted element looks like extreme heat. GM's HPC2 table 18OBDG02 fails the test when the converted value is above 160 °C in 8 of 10 readings at 100 ms, Type B, with more than 10.2 V supply; the 2011 Volt table used 87.5 °C, a raw count below 680, for 1.4 s within a 2 s window over two trips. In GM's 2019 table the pack over-temperature monitor P0A7E is suspended while such short codes are active, because a false hot reading would otherwise trigger it. Mitsubishi calls P0CB4 a short of module sensor [14] on the Outlander PHEV: under 0.12 V, roughly above 125 °C, for 2 s.

causes.label: Signal lead of sensor O shorted to ground in the pack
Thermistor O shorted internally
Input stage of the cell monitoring unit defective

symptoms: Live data showing an implausibly hot module
Strongly reduced battery power with warning lamp
Battery cooling running without obvious need

P0CB5.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor O Circuit High
P0CB5.description: P0CB5 is stored when the input of sensor O sits above its upper voltage limit. An open thermistor, a broken wire or a loose plug lets the pull-up resistor raise the input, so the controller sees a temperature colder than any real pack could be. GM sets it in the HPC2 table 18OBDG02 when 8 of 10 readings at 100 ms intervals come out below −69 °C, Type B, with supply above 10.2 V and intact communication with the battery interface module. The 2011 Volt table drew the line at −40 °C, a raw count above 4,000, for 1.4 s within 2 s, and there one trip sufficed. For the Outlander PHEV, Mitsubishi reads P0CB5 as an open circuit of module sensor [14]: above 3.97 V, below about −62 °C, for 2 s. A plug-in may then warm the pack for nothing or run the engine more; P0CB4 is the low twin.

causes.label: Open lead or unplugged connector of sensor O
Thermistor O open internally
Corroded or loose terminal at the sensing board

symptoms: Pack shown as extremely cold regardless of weather
Less electric power, engine running more on plug-in hybrids

P0CB6.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor O Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0CB6.description: P0CB6 targets a sensor O signal that jitters or jumps instead of changing smoothly. Only GM's later HPC2 tables (16OBDG02 to 19OBDG02) define it: every 100 ms a sample is taken, the absolute steps between ten consecutive samples are summed, and a sum above 10 marks that window as failed. Four failed windows out of five set the code as Type B, so the lamp follows on the second trip; the test needs more than 10.2 V and a working link to the battery interface module. The earlier Volt tables of 2011 and 2012 had no such code for O, and Mitsubishi uses none for its pack sensors. Because the reading can stay inside the valid band, P0CB4 and P0CB5 may never appear. Shaking the harness while watching live data, and the freeze-frame record, help to find a fretting contact or cracked solder joint.

causes.label: Fretting or loose terminal in the sensor O circuit
Cracked solder joint or trace on the sensing board
Chafed lead touching ground only under vibration

symptoms: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Sensor O value jumping in live data

P0CB7.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor P Circuit
P0CB7.description: P0CB7 covers an electrical fault of battery temperature sensor P that the controller cannot pin down as low, high or intermittent. No manufacturer lists this code on a public official server. In GM's 2011 Volt rationality table P is the sixteenth and last sensor, and GM gives it only P0CB8 to P0CBB; Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV treats P as module sensor [15] with rationality, short and open codes. In this block P is the final sensor letter, the next code P0CBC already concerns drive motor cooling. CARB requires the battery temperature sensors to be monitored under section (e)(15.2.3)(A)(iv), with circuit faults and range violations to be told apart per (e)(15.2.1). A missing value of P makes the battery controller act cautiously and lower power. Checking means opening the de-energised pack.

causes.label: Loose or corroded plug of sensor P
Damaged wiring of sensor P inside the pack
Measuring channel for sensor P in the monitoring unit faulty

symptoms: Hybrid or EV warning message
Limited electric power until repaired

P0CB8.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor P Circuit Range/Performance
P0CB8.description: P0CB8 flags sensor P as implausible: its value is electrically fine, but after a long rest it disagrees with the temperature of the other modules. GM runs this comparison in the 2012 Volt table 12OBDG01A only when drive system, external charging and battery conditioning have rested for over 21,600 s, so the whole pack should have settled; 50 of 67 samples more than 25.3 °C from the average give a Type B fault. In the HPC2 table 18OBDG02 the limit is 25.00 °C, sampled every 25 ms for about 1.7 s, and the check is held back by circuit or erratic faults and by lost communication. Mitsubishi uses P0CB8 for module sensor [15] of the Outlander PHEV with a 13 °C limit over 0.32 s after more than 3,600 s soak. Comparing all sensors in live data after an overnight stand shows the outlier.

causes.label: Thermistor P drifted out of calibration
Sensor P detached from its module surface
Real temperature difference of that module, e.g. faulty cell

symptoms: Warning appearing at the first drive after a long stand
Battery output restricted

P0CB9.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor P Circuit Low
P0CB9.description: P0CB9 means the voltage of sensor P has fallen under the valid range. As with the other NTC sensors, low voltage corresponds to high temperature, so a short to ground or a collapsed thermistor makes the module appear to be glowing hot. In GM's HPC2 tables 18OBDG02 and 19OBDG02 the code is set after 8 of 10 readings above 160 °C at 100 ms spacing, Type B, two trips, once system voltage exceeds 10.2 V and the battery interface module communicates. The 2011 Volt table already contained it with 87.5 °C, a raw count below 680, held 1.4 s within 2 s. Mitsubishi treats P0CB9 as a short of module sensor [15] of the Outlander PHEV, below 0.12 V for 2 s, lists no fail-safe function and names battery module or cell monitoring unit as the parts to replace. A genuinely hot pack is reported by P0A7E.

causes.label: Sensor P signal shorted to ground
Thermistor P internally shorted
Damaged input of the cell monitoring unit for sensor P

symptoms: Module P shown as extremely hot in live data
Severe power limitation with warning lamp

P0CBA.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor P Circuit High
P0CBA.description: P0CBA appears when the signal of sensor P rises above its upper voltage limit, the typical picture of an open circuit: without a closed path through the thermistor, the pull-up resistor drives the input high and the computed temperature drops to an absurd value. GM's 2019 HPC2 table 19OBDG02 fails it when 8 of 10 readings at 100 ms fall below −69 °C, Type B, provided supply exceeds 10.2 V and the battery interface control module is online. In the 2011 Volt table the limit was −40 °C, a raw count above 4,000, held 1.4 s within 2 s, and a single trip set the code. On the Outlander PHEV, Mitsubishi files P0CBA as an open circuit of module sensor [15] once the voltage stays above 3.97 V for 2 s. Cold-weather strategies such as pack heating may then start needlessly; P0CB9 is the matching low code.

causes.label: Open circuit or disconnected plug of sensor P
Thermistor P broken internally
Spread or corroded terminal on the sensing board

symptoms: Very low battery temperature displayed on a warm day
Battery heater or engine running more than usual

P0CBB.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor P Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0CBB.description: P0CBB is about short dropouts or spikes in the signal of sensor P that do not last long enough, or go far enough, to trip the low or high code. GM defines it in the HPC2 tables 16OBDG02 to 19OBDG02 and judges how restless the signal is: within each window of ten samples taken 100 ms apart the size of every change is added up, a total above 10 fails the window, and four bad windows in five produce the code, Type B, two trips. Enable conditions are more than 10.2 V and communication with the battery interface module. Neither the 2011/2012 Volt tables nor Mitsubishi know this fault type for sensor P. An intermittent contact often shows up only with vibration or temperature change, so the freeze frame and a road test with live data matter more than a static resistance check.

causes.label: Intermittent contact at the sensor P plug
Hairline crack in the sensing board near the sensor P input
Unstable reference or ground of the monitoring unit

symptoms: Intermittent warning that may clear by itself
Erratic sensor P reading in live data

P0CBC.title: Drive Motor A Coolant Temperature Sensor Circuit
P0CBC.description: P0CBC is the general code for the sensor that measures coolant temperature in the cooling loop of drive motor A. Volvo and Polestar document it as P0CBC62 in the inverter module IEM of the Polestar 2 and the XC40/C40 Recharge (Technical Journals 37523 and 37521 from 2025): failure type 62 marks a signal comparison fault, and the vehicle displays a propulsion service message. In many of these cars the root cause was a defective check valve in a coolant hose, not the module. The phase transistor temperatures then swing widely while driving; at 80–100 °C the IEM sets a temperature code and freewheels, which stops a single-motor car and halves power on dual motors. Before replacing the IEM, plot those temperatures and renew the valve hose. CARB section (e)(15.2.3)(B)(ii) covers inverter cooling inputs.

causes.label: Faulty one-way valve in the drive unit coolant hose (Volvo/Polestar TJ 37521/37523)
Low coolant or trapped air in the drive motor loop
Sensor or wiring fault in the temperature circuit
Internal fault of the inverter module

symptoms: Propulsion system service message
Loss of drive power, car may stop on single-motor versions
Half power only on dual-motor versions

P0CBD.title: Drive Motor A Coolant Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P0CBD.description: P0CBD reports that the coolant temperature sensor of drive motor A gives a believable voltage but an implausible temperature. GM uses it on the 2013 eAssist models, where the drive motor is the belt-driven motor generator with its own small cooling loop. Table 13OBDG05C runs the check once per key cycle after an engine-off period of more than 21,600 s: the loop sensor is compared with the mean of stator temperature, intake air temperature and transmission fluid temperature, and a difference above 25 °C in 50 of 62 samples at 100 ms is a Type B fault. The test is skipped while stator sensor codes P0A2B–P0A2D, intake air or transmission fluid sensor codes, the sensor's own P0CBE/P0CBF or CAN faults U0100/U0101 are active. A drifting sensor is the likely cause; the motor generator may be limited meanwhile.

causes.label: Coolant temperature sensor drifted out of its curve
Added resistance from a corroded connector
One of the comparison sensors (stator, intake air, transmission oil) reading wrongly

symptoms: Check-engine lamp after the second faulty trip
Reduced electric assist or regeneration

P0CBE.title: Drive Motor A Coolant Temperature Sensor Circuit Low
P0CBE.description: P0CBE says the coolant temperature input of drive motor A is below its valid range, meaning the sensor resistance has become very small. GM's 2013 eAssist table 13OBDG05C sets the code when the raw reading is under 100.9 Ω, which equals 120 °C, in 50 of 62 samples taken every 100 ms with the vehicle in run/crank; it is a Type B fault, so the lamp comes on after the second trip. Such a low value is usually a shorted sensor or a signal line rubbing through to ground. GM's preliminary information PIC5720A for 2012–2013 LaCrosse and Regal, 2013 Malibu Eco and 2014 Impala Eco with eAssist describes exactly that: a misrouted harness touching the crank, A/C compressor pulley or belt, together with C027B and C0040 and a humming noise. Its partner for an open circuit is P0CBF.

causes.label: Harness rubbing on crank or compressor pulley or belt (GM PIC5720A)
Coolant temperature sensor shorted internally
Loop genuinely very hot, e.g. pump or coolant fault

symptoms: Check-engine lamp, possibly with ABS or brake assist warning
Hum or buzz from the right front
Electric assist restricted

P0CBF.title: Drive Motor A Coolant Temperature Sensor Circuit High
P0CBF.description: P0CBF is the code for an excessive signal from the coolant temperature sensor of drive motor A. With an NTC element a very high resistance stands for extreme cold, so in practice an open sensor, a broken wire or a disconnected plug is behind it. In GM's 2013 eAssist table 13OBDG05C the code is set when the raw value exceeds 176,962 Ω, the equivalent of −40 °C, in 50 of 62 samples at 100 ms with ignition in run/crank, Type B, two trips. Because −40 °C is a real if rare ambient temperature, the check uses a resistance far beyond the normal working curve. With the loop temperature unknown, the system has to fall back on substitute values and may scale back the electric assist. The codes P0CBD and P0CC2 rely on this sensor and are blocked while P0CBF is present; P0CBE is its low counterpart.

causes.label: Open signal or return wire, or unplugged sensor
Sensor element open internally
Corroded pins at sensor or control module

symptoms: Check-engine lamp after two trips
Coolant temperature of the motor shown at minimum value

P0CC0.title: Drive Motor A Coolant Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent
P0CC0.description: P0CC0 is meant for a coolant temperature signal of drive motor A that drops out or jumps for short moments. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM's 2013 eAssist table, the most detailed public source for this sensor, monitors it only with P0CBD for plausibility and P0CBE/P0CBF for out-of-range values; Volvo and Polestar report P0CBC with failure type 62. CARB section (e)(15.2.1) asks for circuit and range faults of inputs to be detected, and (e)(15.2.3)(B)(ii) extends this to the cooling of the inverter. A sporadic code typically stems from a loose terminal, a chafed wire that touches metal only on bumps, or water in the connector. Since the reading normally recovers, the lamp may go out again; live data recorded during a drive help to catch the moment of the fault.

causes.label: Loose or spread terminal in the sensor connector
Chafed wire making contact only on bumps
Moisture in the connector

symptoms: Warning lamp that appears and disappears
Jumping coolant temperature value in live data

P0CC1.title: Drive Motor A Coolant Pump Control Circuit/Open
P0CC1.description: P0CC1 concerns the control circuit of the electric pump that moves coolant through the loop of drive motor A, here specifically an open circuit. GM documents it for the 2013 eAssist hybrids, where the table 13OBDG05C calls the part the motor generator coolant pump: the output driver reports an open-circuit status, and 20 of 25 checks at 250 ms intervals with the vehicle in run/crank and the pump commanded off fail the test, Type B, two trips. Checking in the off state lets the driver detect a missing load without running the pump. A broken wire, a corroded pump connector or an open motor winding are typical causes. With the pump not reachable, the motor generator cannot be cooled actively, so the system is likely to limit assist and charging; the short codes P0CC3 and P0CC4 belong to the same circuit.

causes.label: Broken control or supply wire to the pump
Corroded or unplugged pump connector
Open winding inside the pump motor

symptoms: Check-engine lamp after two trips
Less electric assist and regeneration

P0CC2.title: Drive Motor A Coolant Pump Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0CC2.description: P0CC2 judges whether the pump for drive motor A actually moves coolant, not only whether its wiring is intact. GM's 2013 eAssist table 13OBDG05C infers flow from temperature: when the model predicts more than 17 °C between the jacket coolant of the motor generator and the coolant reaching the loop sensor, a running pump should make the sensor warm up quickly. If its rate of change stays at 0.25 °C per second or less 20 s after the pump was switched on, the test fails, Type B, two trips, with over 10 V supply. The check is blocked by pump circuit codes P0CC1/P0CC3/P0CC4, by the loop sensor codes P0CBD to P0CBF and by stator sensor codes P0A2B to P0A2D. A seized or air-locked pump, low coolant or a blocked hose are typical; CARB section (e)(15.2.2) requires such functional checks of output components.

causes.label: Air in the motor generator cooling loop, often after service
Worn or seized pump impeller
Low coolant level or kinked or blocked hose

symptoms: Check-engine lamp
Electric assist reduced as the motor generator heats up

P0CC3.title: Drive Motor A Coolant Pump Control Circuit Low
P0CC3.description: P0CC3 indicates that the control line of the drive motor A coolant pump is pulled to ground. GM lists it for the 2013 eAssist cars in table 13OBDG05C: the hardware status of the output driver signals a low-circuit fault, and 20 of 25 samples at 250 ms with the pump commanded off and the vehicle in run/crank fail the test, Type B, so the MIL is lit after the second trip. Typical are chafed insulation where the harness passes brackets or the engine, or a pump with an internal short. Depending on how the driver stage is built, a grounded line can also leave the pump running permanently or stop it, so either constant pump noise or missing cooling is possible. Compared with the open-circuit code P0CC1 and the short-to-voltage code P0CC4, the repair focuses on finding the point of ground contact.

causes.label: Chafed control wire touching ground
Internal short in the pump
Faulty output stage in the control module

symptoms: Check-engine lamp after two trips
Pump running constantly or not at all
Reduced electric assist

P0CC4.title: Drive Motor A Coolant Pump Control Circuit High
P0CC4.description: P0CC4 stands for a control line of the drive motor A coolant pump that is held at supply voltage or overloaded. In GM's 2013 eAssist table 13OBDG05C the output driver reports a high-circuit status, and unlike the open and low checks this one runs while the pump is commanded on; 20 failures in 25 samples at 250 ms in run/crank set a Type B code, two trips. Sampling with the output switched on lets the driver recognise excess current or a voltage that should not be there. Causes include a control wire chafed against a battery-positive feed, a pump drawing too much current because of a jammed rotor, or water in the connector. The output stage normally switches off to protect itself, so the pump stops and the motor generator loses active cooling; P0CC3 and P0CC1 are the other circuit codes of this pump.

causes.label: Control wire shorted to a voltage-carrying line
Jammed pump drawing excess current
Water ingress in the pump connector

symptoms: Check-engine lamp after two trips
Pump silent when it should run

P0CC5.title: 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor A/B Correlation
P0CC5.description: P0CC5 compares the two current sensors of the 14 V power module, the DC/DC converter that feeds the 12 V network from the high-voltage battery. In GM's 2013 eAssist table 13OBDG05C, where the unit is the accessory power module (APM), sensor A measures the input and sensor B the output side. The module computes an input power, multiplies it by an efficiency factor taken from a table (0.99 down to 0.90) and compares the result with the power derived from the output side; a gap above 0.4 kW for 3.75 s within a 5 s window, at 9 to 32 V and with the input power inside the enabling window the table ties to 1.25 kW, is a Type B fault. The check is suspended while the single-sensor codes P0A88/P0A89 or P0C9E/P0C9F are active. One drifting sensor is the usual reason, and a 12 V battery that stays poorly charged is a typical sign.

causes.label: Offset or gain drift of one current sensor
Internal fault of the power module, e.g. real efficiency loss
Calibration or software fault in the module

symptoms: Check-engine lamp after the second faulty trip
12 V battery not fully charged or low-voltage warning

P0CC6.title: Charge Port Door A Open Request Switch Wake-Up Circuit
P0CC6.description: On plug-in vehicles the button that asks for the charge flap to open must also be able to rouse a sleeping control module, so it drives a separate wake-up line besides its normal signal. P0CC6 records that these two signals disagree. GM documents the code for the 2011 Chevrolet Volt, where the hybrid control module 2 (VICM) checks two cases: wake-up active although the switch reads released, and switch pressed with no wake-up seen. Both are filtered over 50 ms samples and stored as Type B after two trips with the warning lamp. The test is skipped while P0CC7, P0CC9 or P0CCA is active, so P0CC6 points to the wake-up wire or the switch contact itself. The driver mostly notices that pressing the button sometimes does not open the flap.

causes.label: Open, chafed or shorted wake-up wire between switch and control module
Worn or contaminated contact in the open request switch
Corroded or loose pins at the switch or module connector
Faulty wake-up input inside the control module

symptoms: Charge flap opens only after several presses or not at all
Warning lamp after two trips (GM Volt)
Possible extra drain on the 12 V battery if the module is kept awake

P0CC7.title: Charge Port Door A Open Request Switch Circuit
P0CC7.description: P0CC7 is the general circuit fault of the button that requests opening of charge flap A. GM reads this switch as a percentage of its reference and expects defined states; on the 2011 to 2013 Chevrolet Volt the code sets when the reading sits in a forbidden band between 65.9 and 81.6 percent, which indicates a wrong resistance, for instance a damaged switch or a partly broken wire. Six bad readings out of eight (50 ms steps in 2011/2012, 500 ms in the 2013 table) trigger it, and it is a Type B code with the lamp after two trips. Hard shorts are split off into P0CC9 (to ground) and P0CCA (to battery voltage); unstable signals belong to P0CCB. In daily use the flap may ignore the button, while opening via the key or screen can still work.

causes.label: Open request switch with wrong internal resistance
Partly broken wire or corroded connector raising circuit resistance
Moisture in the switch housing
Faulty switch input in the control module

symptoms: Charge flap does not open with the button
Warning lamp after two trips (GM Volt)
Opening via key, app or screen still possible on some models

P0CC8.title: Charge Port Door A Open Request Switch Circuit Performance
P0CC8.description: P0CC8 covers a plausibility fault of the charge flap A open request switch: the signal is electrically within limits, yet its behaviour makes no sense, for example a button that reports pressed for far too long or never changes state over many wake-ups. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM's Volt tables of 2011 to 2013 monitor the same switch only for invalid range, low and high (P0CC7, P0CC9, P0CCA), so the performance check is not used there. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15) requires rationality checks only for inputs that affect emissions or serve another diagnostic, which explains why such comfort inputs are often left out. A GM patent shows the typical layout, in which the release button makes the controller energize the flap actuator. Expect a flap that reacts erratically to the button.

causes.label: Mechanically sticking or jammed open request switch
Worn switch contact giving an implausible signal
Wiring fault that keeps the signal in an unexpected state

symptoms: Charge flap opens unexpectedly or ignores the button
Message about the charge flap in the instrument cluster

P0CC9.title: Charge Port Door A Open Request Switch Circuit Low
P0CC9.description: P0CC9 means the open request switch of charge flap A reads lower than any valid state, which typically results from the signal wire touching ground or from a switch that has failed short. In the Chevrolet Volt tables of 2011 to 2013, GM sets it once the reading drops under 22.9 percent of the reference in six of eight samples; the code is Type B, so the warning lamp follows after two consecutive trips. The monitor belongs to the hybrid control module 2 (VICM). The opposite fault, a reading above 94.5 percent, is P0CCA, and a value stuck between valid states is P0CC7. Because a grounded signal may look like a permanently pressed button, the flap can fail to respond or the module may stay awake longer than intended.

causes.label: Signal wire chafed through to body ground
Open request switch shorted internally
Water in the switch connector creating a leakage path to ground

symptoms: Charge flap does not react to the button
Warning lamp after two trips (GM Volt)

P0CCA.title: Charge Port Door A Open Request Switch Circuit High
P0CCA.description: With P0CCA the control module sees the charge flap A open request switch signal above its highest valid level. Depending on the circuit, a wire shorted to battery voltage or an interrupted ground or switch path pushes the reading up. GM's Volt monitor from 2011 onward flags it when more than 94.5 percent of the reference is measured in six of eight samples, then stores it as a Type B code with the lamp after two trips; the 2013 table stretches the sample spacing to 500 ms. Low readings below 22.9 percent go to P0CC9 instead, and an invalid middle value to P0CC7. Since a high reading usually looks like a button that is never pressed, the typical complaint is a charge flap that cannot be opened from the switch.

causes.label: Signal wire shorted to a 12 V supply
Interrupted ground or switch return path
Pin pushed back in the connector

symptoms: Charge flap cannot be opened with the button
Warning lamp after two trips (GM Volt)

P0CCB.title: Charge Port Door A Open Request Switch Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0CCB.description: P0CCB flags a charge flap A open request switch whose signal jumps between states without a matching press, or drops out briefly. Such signals usually come from loose terminals, a cracked solder joint in the switch or a harness that flexes with a door or body panel. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's Volt tables of 2011 and 2012 cover the same switch only with P0CC7, P0CC9 and P0CCA, which use six of eight samples as a filter and would hide short dropouts. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15) makes intermittent checks mandatory only for emission-related inputs, so a comfort switch like this one rarely carries one. The GM charge port patent shows how the button press leads the controller to fire the flap actuator. The driver sees the flap answer only now and then.

causes.label: Loose or spread terminal at the switch or module connector
Cracked solder joint or worn contact inside the switch
Harness damaged where it flexes with a door or panel

symptoms: Charge flap opens only occasionally when the button is pressed
Fault comes and goes, often with temperature or road vibration

P0CCC.title: Charge Port Door A Position Sensor Circuit
P0CCC.description: The position sensor of charge flap A tells the vehicle whether the flap is open or shut; GM has patented a version in which a magnet on the flap acts on a magnetic sensor in the housing. P0CCC is the general circuit code for this sensor. On the 2011 to 2013 Chevrolet Volt it sets when the reading lands in the invalid window of 65.9 to 81.6 percent of reference in six of eight samples, as a Type B code with the lamp after two trips. GM uses the flap state as an enable condition for the control pilot check P0CF4, which is why the sensor is part of the OBD system there; GM's 2016 hybrid table no longer lists these flap codes. Short circuits have their own codes, P0CCE (low) and P0CCF (high). The driver may see a false flap-open message or a charging refusal.

causes.label: Faulty flap position sensor or switch
Sensor or its harness pigtail not fully seated in the housing
Damaged wire or corroded connector in the sensor circuit

symptoms: Flap-open message although the flap is closed
Warning lamp after two trips (GM Volt)
Charging or charge pilot checks may be blocked

P0CCD.title: Charge Port Door A Position Sensor Circuit Performance
P0CCD.description: P0CCD is set when the charge flap A position signal is electrically valid but does not fit what the flap should be doing, for example a state that disagrees with the last commanded movement. GM bulletin 25-NA-049 (March 2025) names the code for the Ultium models Cadillac Lyriq 2023 to 2025, Chevrolet Blazer EV and Equinox EV 2024 to 2025, and Cadillac Optiq and Escalade IQ 2025: drivers see a Service High Voltage message, the cause is attributed to software, and dealers are told to reflash the BECM (battery energy control module) through vehicle wide programming without replacing parts. Porsche describes a related hardware case for the Taycan, where a wrong end-position signal locked the opposite flap and new harnesses fixed it. Circuit faults proper are P0CCC, P0CCE and P0CCF.

causes.label: Software anomaly in the battery control module (GM Ultium, bulletin 25-NA-049)
Position sensor giving a wrong end-position signal
Faulty harness between flap module and control unit
Flap not reaching its end position because of mechanical binding

symptoms: Service High Voltage message (GM Ultium models)
Flap status shown wrongly; another flap may be locked

P0CCE.title: Charge Port Door A Position Sensor Circuit Low
P0CCE.description: P0CCE reports that the charge flap A position sensor signal has fallen below its lowest valid level, the classic sign of a signal wire shorted to ground or a sensor that has failed short. GM documents it for the 2011 to 2013 Chevrolet Volt: the hybrid control module 2 sets it when the reading is under 22.9 percent of reference in six of eight samples, and as a Type B code the lamp comes on after two trips. While it is active, GM suspends dependent tests such as the control pilot check P0CF4 and the flap opening check P0CD2. The high-side counterpart is P0CCF, the invalid middle window P0CCC. For the driver this mostly means a wrong flap status in the display and, depending on software, blocked charging.

causes.label: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Position sensor shorted internally
Water in the flap area or sensor connector

symptoms: Wrong flap status in the display
Warning lamp after two trips (GM Volt)
Charging may be refused

P0CCF.title: Charge Port Door A Position Sensor Circuit High
P0CCF.description: P0CCF stands for a charge flap A position sensor signal above its highest valid level. A signal wire touching a 12 V feed, or an interrupted sensor ground that lets the input float upwards, are the usual explanations. In GM's Chevrolet Volt tables from 2011 to 2013 the threshold is 94.5 percent of reference, confirmed in six of eight samples; the 2013 table samples at 500 ms. The code is Type B, so the lamp lights after the second trip with the fault. As with P0CCE, an active P0CCF stops GM's dependent tests P0CF4 and P0CD2 from running. Low readings are P0CCE, plausibility problems P0CCD. A driver typically gets a flap status that never changes or a message that the flap is open.

causes.label: Sensor signal wire shorted to a 12 V feed
Interrupted sensor ground or open sensor
Unplugged or damaged sensor connector

symptoms: Flap status stuck or shown as open
Warning lamp after two trips (GM Volt)

P0CD0.title: Charge Port Door A Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0CD0.description: P0CD0 completes the position sensor group of charge flap A: the module sees the flap signal flicker or drop out for moments, without a lasting open, short or implausible state. Loose connector terminals, a sensor that is not held firmly in its seat, or a harness strained by the flap mechanism are the usual triggers. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Two official sources describe faults of the same part: Porsche replaced the flap harnesses on the 2020 Taycan because a faulty sensor signal misjudged the end position, and GM patented a magnet and sensor pair that reports whether the flap is shut. The steady faults have their own codes, P0CCC, P0CCE and P0CCF, and P0CCD covers plausibility. A driver may see the flap status switch back and forth or get sporadic charging warnings.

causes.label: Loose terminal in the position sensor connector
Harness to the flap module chafed or under strain
Sensor or magnet not held firmly in its mounting

symptoms: Flap status in the display changes without reason
Sporadic charging or flap warnings

P0CD1.title: Charge Port Door A Unlock Control Circuit
P0CD1.description: P0CD1 is the circuit fault of the output that releases charge flap A, normally a relay or driver that briefly powers the latch actuator. A GM patent shows such an actuator retracting a post so the spring-loaded flap can pop open. On the 2011 to 2013 Chevrolet Volt the hybrid control module 2 relies on the fault status its driver reports and covers two cases: short to ground, judged while the unlock is commanded, and a short to 12 V or an open line, judged while it is not, using sample counts such as 64 of 80 at 50 ms. It is a Type B code with the lamp after two trips, and an active P0CD1 blocks the opening check P0CD2. Split low and high codes (P0CD3, P0CD4) are not used there. Result for the driver: the flap stays shut.

causes.label: Unlock actuator coil open or shorted
Faulty charge flap relay or its control wire
Chafed or corroded wiring to the actuator
Output driver in the control module damaged

symptoms: Charge flap does not unlock
Warning lamp after two trips (GM Volt)
Emergency release needed to reach the charge socket

P0CD2.title: Charge Port Door A Unlock Control Circuit Performance
P0CD2.description: P0CD2 is a functional test: after commanding charge flap A to unlock, the module waits for the position sensor to report the flap open. GM documents it for the Chevrolet Volt. The 2011 table allows 5 seconds, the 2012 and 2013 tables 13 seconds, and the 2013 version only runs above minus 12 °C.
